newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Nationwide defies conversion move.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Nationwide defies conversion move.

text.p: Britain's largest building society, the Nationwide, on Wednesday posted an annual pretax profits fall of 33 percent to 264.8 million pounds ($433.5 million) after carrying out its pledge to return 200 million pounds to members.
"This is excellent news for Nationwide customers and underlines the commitment made last year to give back 200 million pounds to customers through better rates," said chief executive Brian Davis.
Nationwide also said it will beat off attempts by some of its members to force it to convert to bank status and float on the stock exchange.

It has remained is committed to maintaining its mutual status despite the recent rash of building societies rushing to the stock market. The most recent of these was the Halifax, which floated on the London market last week.
Members for Conversion, a pressure group run by Michael Hardern, is putting up five candidates in elections to the Nationwide board.
"We will beat him," said Nationwide finance director Alistair Dales in an interview. "All we need to do is make sure the members use their votes. We must not be complacent."
Dales added that if the five candidates in favour of conversion were to be elected to the board, the Society would probably hold a referendum of the membership.
"We would certainly have to revisit the decision the board made some 18 months ago to remain a strong mutual," Dales said.
Nationwide's assets grew by 7.5 percent to 40.5 billion pounds while its tier one capital ratio grew to 11.1 percent from 11.0 percent.
Dales insisted that the Nationwide's strategy of remaining independent and returning value to members was sustainable.
"When we embarked upon this campaign, we stress- tested it under a number of scenarios," Dales said. "The critical thing was to maintain the capital ratio."
Dales said the Nationwide could operate on even lower margins than at present though he declined to give details.
"We could force margins down if we wished to and they (the banks) have to pay dividends to their shareholders. That's the conflict they have that we don't have."

Dales said the housing market recovery was patchy and was cautious of predicting further improvement until it became clear whether mortgage interest tax relief (MIRAS) was to be abolished in the coming budget.

"It's just starting to pick up but it's very patchy. If you add the recent rise in mortgage rates (the Nationwide left its rate unchanged) to the possible abolition of MIRAS, that would have a significant effect on the cost of paying back a mortgage."
Dales said that the Nationwide would prefer MIRAS or something similar remained to give some support to the housing market.
He repeated that Nationwide would continue to look to organic growth rather than by mergers.

"We are not interested in merging with anybody or acquiring anybody," Dales said. "We grew organically by nearly eight percent last year and we expect to grow organically to be a 50 billion pounds institution by the year 2000."
